entries.title: keep main's platform pins one release behind so every commit agrees with its lockfile
entries.body:
The release commit moved the optionalDependencies pins to the new version while the lockfile entries they resolve to describe tarballs that exist only after release.yml publishes the tag, so main disagreed with its own lockfile and CI's lint job was red on every release commit.

release-pr.yml now bumps only the version. The release job stamps the pins with scripts/pin-platform-packages.mjs just before npm pack and verifies the packed package.json, and the lockfile job moves the pins and their lockfile entries together in one pull request. The lockfile check no longer skips the Release PR and tags.

entries.title: httpFetch, a blocking HTTP/1.1 client for CLIs
entries.body:
`nish/net/http-client` fetches an http or https URL from a command-line program. `httpFetch(request, options)` covers a one-shot request, and `HttpClient` keeps one connection alive across requests.

It dials through the std DNS resolver and makes a non-blocking connect over each address within `connectTimeoutMs`. https goes over the std TLS 1.3 client, and the server's chain is checked against trusted roots with RFC 6125 host matching: `rootsPemPath`, else SSL_CERT_FILE / SSL_CERT_DIR / the system bundles. There is no insecure switch. A missing root store is refused before any byte is sent.

- **Timeouts and the body.** `readTimeoutMs` bounds each wait. `totalTimeoutMs` bounds the whole fetch, redirects and the body reader included. The body reader hands out bytes as they arrive, so Server-Sent Events and JSON lines can be parsed while they stream.
- **Keep-alive.** A connection is reused only when the previous response was fully read and nothing is left in the parser, the TLS layer or the idle socket. That closes response-queue poisoning. An idempotent request lost before any byte is retried once.
- **Redirects** are off by default, and same-origin only unless cross-origin is allowed. Authorization, Proxy-Authorization and Cookie are dropped across origins, and https→http is always refused.
- **Proxies.** HTTPS_PROXY tunnels through CONNECT and HTTP_PROXY sends the absolute form, both honouring NO_PROXY. httpoxy is guarded against. Proxy userinfo goes to the proxy only.
- **Error text** never echoes userinfo, a query or a fragment: URLs are named from their parsed form, and text that does not parse is not echoed at all.

The tests are pinned by a mechanical mutation sweep. Every remaining survivor is argued in docs/security/http-client.md, which also records the threat model and HF-1 to HF-9. examples/http-get-json.ts GETs a live HTTPS JSON API; a run through this environment's proxy to api.github.com is in the PR.

Tests: tests/link/net_http_fetch (+ _f64, _tls)
Refs: docs/security/http-client.md, docs/guide/using-nish/http-client.md
Part of #994

entries.title: round on SSE4.1 when the CPU has it
entries.body:
On the default x86-64 target (the SSE2 baseline), `Math.floor`, `Math.ceil`, `Math.trunc` and the floor inside `Math.round` lowered to calls of libm through the GOT. They now call the runtime's `nish_floor`, `nish_ceil` and `nish_trunc`, which are one `roundsd` on any CPU with SSE4.1. The default target is not raised, so a binary still runs on baseline x86-64.

A module that rounds registers an internal constructor at priority 101. The constructor passes libm's `floor`, `ceil` and `trunc` to `nish_round_init`. The runtime asks the CPU once:
- With SSE4.1, it keeps nothing, and each call is the inline instruction.
- Without SSE4.1, or under `NISH_SIMD=scalar`, it keeps the libm pointers, and each call jumps to libm, with the same bits as before.

The runtime names no libm symbol, so a C host, or a program that never rounds, still links without `-lm`.

Unchanged:
- `--cpu x86-64-v3` builds are byte-identical to before.
- aarch64 and wasm lowering do not change, and a build with no `--target` dispatches only on an x86-64 host.

`tests/cases/math_rounding` pins every edge of the four functions (±0, NaN, the infinities, the subnormals, 2^52 and beyond) against Node, and runs again under `NISH_SIMD=scalar` so CI covers the libm path.
metrics: round kernel 513 ms vs 574/566 ms median (-9.7%), min 484 vs 536/538, 25 interleaved pinned runs; A/A noise band 8 ms median, 2 ms min; --cpu x86-64-v3 byte-identical; NISH_SIMD=scalar fallback +11%

entries.title: setNice refuses a raise and values outside 0..19
entries.body:
setNice passed its argument straight to setpriority, which the kernel clamps to -20..19, so a privileged process could raise its own priority. It now takes 0..19 only: a value outside that range answers -22 (EINVAL) with no system call, and a value below the current nice value answers -13 (EACCES) with no setpriority call. The refusal applies to root too.

setIdlePriority is unchanged. It already only lowers, moving the process to SCHED_IDLE on Linux and answering -95 elsewhere.

entries.title: tune the portable SHA-256 path
entries.body:
SHA-256's portable compression, which every CPU without the SHA extensions runs, now has its 64 rounds written out with each round constant as an immediate. A block costs one bounds check, and words 0 to 14 each load as one load and a byte swap. Every read stays checked: nothing imports nish:unsafe, so hashing never makes a caller reach `unsafe`. The private sha256Compress keeps its name, signature and once-per-block meaning, and HMAC-SHA256, PBKDF2 and HS256 pick the speed-up up with no API change.

bench/sha256 times sha256 on 64 B, 1 KiB and 1 MiB inputs and an HS256 sign+verify in ns/op. Before any timing, each build must print a pinned known checksum per case.
metrics: sha256 64 B 1.13x (band ±2.3%), 1 KiB 1.30x (±2.4%), 1 MiB 1.37x (±4.2%), HS256 sign+verify 1.22x (±0.2%), medians over 12 interleaved rounds against main, 4-core Xeon @ 2.10GHz

entries.title: read PgBatcher rows and int arrays in binary
entries.body:
* docs(plan): plan binary PgBatcher results and int array decoding

Two stages in std/net/postgres.ts: PgBatcher binary results with the
routing ordinal read in binary, then a one-dimensional int2/int4/int8
binary array walker. Acceptance criteria are in the plan.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Haiku 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01L7QsVLAZQ6cZbBtbnc92LF

* feat(net): read PgBatcher rows in binary with PgBatchConfig.binary

A PgBatcher built with PgBatchConfig.binary set opens each batch with
bindStartBinary, so every row comes in binary, and reads the routing
ordinal with binaryInt. Its refusals are the ones a text batch makes,
and binary.failed is saved and restored around the ordinal read, so the
caller's own decoding is left as it was. A batch that leaves binary
false is byte-identical to before.

The link test covers a binary take's Bind, its ordinals, the caller's
binary.failed, and text and NULL ordinals refused. The live binary
scenario reads the same creation times through a binary batch and a
text batch.

Refs: docs/security/postgres.md (PG-14)
Tests: tests/link/std_postgres_batch, tests/postgres/live binary batch

* feat(net): read one-dimensional int2, int4 and int8 binary arrays

PgBinaryArray walks a one-dimensional int2[], int4[] or int8[] column
read in binary format. It checks the array header (ndim 0 or 1, hasnull
0 or 1, element OID 20, 21 or 23) and each element's length word against
the element's size before it reads any bytes, and it ends with
PG_ARRAY_END only when the column is consumed exactly. Truncated,
over-counted and malformed arrays refuse with PG_ARRAY_BAD and set the
PgBinary failed flag. Multi-dimensional arrays, text[] and numeric[]
still come back in text format.

Tests: tests/link/std_postgres, tests/postgres/live binary

entries.title: link the Nish runner's programs under the suite's profile, in three shards
entries.body:
The golden runner written in Nish linked every tests/link program under
the speed profile, -O3 with LTO, where tests/run.js links all but a listed
few under --profile debug. The native link was most of each program's
time, and CI's `runner` job hit its 15-minute limit on whichever shard drew
a slow machine. The runner now picks the profile the same way, and the
list of programs that keep the speed profile, with the reason for each,
moves out of tests/run.js into tests/speed-link.txt, which both harnesses
read. The profile changes the link, never the IR, so every golden and
expected.ir check is unchanged. The job deals the corpus three ways
instead of two.
metrics: runner job corpus step 3.9, 6.4 and 4.0 min over three shards, against 8.1 and >13.9 min over two (run 40997535378); the 32 net_tls programs on 4 cores, 107 s before and 63 s after
